title: ‘Economic sadism’ if RBA hikes: union boss
full_text:
A leading union figure has accused the Reserve Bank of misdiagnosing the causes of inflation, putting the labour movement at odds with economists warning of the risks from government spending forecast to grow twice as fast as the economy this year.
Ahead of crucial inflation figures to be released on Wednesday that will inform the RBA’s interest-rate decision next week, Health Services Union national secretary Dustin Halse said the central bank “should not hike again”.
“Another round of hikes would be aggressive economic sadism,” Mr Halse told The Australian.
He accused the RBA of “not giving enough weight” to supporting full employment, which is part of its dual mandate.
The debate on government spending comes as new Greens leader David Shoebridge is set to unveil a $22bn policy to raise the tax-free threshold from $18,200 to $26,000.
“That’s more than $1000 back in the pocket of almost every working Australian,” Senator Shoebridge will say in a speech to the National Press Club in Canberra on Wednesday, according to a copy of his speech.
The big spending policy – to be paid for by higher taxes for fossil fuel companies – would also see a $1000 yearly boost to the pension, JobSeeker and other income-support payments.
“Some people will tell you that’s inflationary,” Senator Shoebridge will say. “The 1 per cent and their spinners want you to ignore another key driver of inflation: the surge in corporate profits flooding through their part of the economy, from corporations that don’t pay their fair share of tax.” With the government weighing spending cuts in the upcoming mid-year budget update amid warnings that it was contributing to inflation, Mr Halse said any cuts should not come from the care economy.
“Start with the tax breaks and subsidies handed to corporate Australia, the same businesses that have been setting the prices,” Mr Halse said.
“The RBA has inflicted real pain on people who are the victims of higher prices, not the ones setting them.
“Interest rates are a blunt instrument, the RBA has misdiagnosed what’s driving inflation, and the effectiveness of further hikes is highly debatable.” Mr Halse’s refusal to countenance reductions in public spending in the care economy is a sentiment backed by most Labor MPs, complicating Dr Chalmers’ push to find spending cuts in MYEFO.
Labor MP Julie-Ann Campbell said on Tuesday the government needed to “throw the kitchen sink” at lowering government spending, as long as it did not come at the expense of cost-of-living relief. “These are important, as well as that strong fiscal economic management,” said Ms Campbell, the member for the Brisbane seat of Moreton.
Dr Chalmers used parliament’s question time on Tuesday to defend government spending levels, arguing that growth in public demand had halved over the past year. “Public demand is coming up in our economy, but private final demand growth tripled in that year compared to the year before,” the Treasurer said.
Despite the government spending more than it has saved, both Dr Chalmers and Finance Minister Katy Gallagher talked up the $180bn of savings the government had made since it was elected.
Senator Gallagher said opposition from the Coalition and the Greens to the Albanese government’s “modest” overhaul of private health insurance, removing the higher rebate for over 65s introduced by the Howard government, showed how hard it was to secure savings.
“The opposition demands saves and then you bring saves, sensible and modest saves, to the parliament and they say, ‘no thanks, you should be spending more on that’,” the Finance Minister said.
Nomura chief economist Andrew Ticehurst said that while demand for technology materials would keep inflation high, government spending was still clearly an issue.
“The RBA does have a stronger public spending number than economic growth,” Mr Ticehurst said.
He noted that the central bank had forecast 3.2 per cent growth in public demand for the year to December compared with 1.4 per cent economic growth for the same period.
“So public demand is still contributing to total demand and that is inflationary and making the Reserve Bank’s job harder,” Mr Ticehurst said.
“Public demand is still a story. There is a political overlay to all this.” He said Australia was probably heading towards some degree of stagflation. “We are halfway to stagflation,” he said. “We are not quite there yet – it’s not a complete disaster.” The consensus of economists has Wednesday’s inflation data showing the Reserve Bank’s preferred measure – the trimmed or core number – at 1 per cent for the September quarter and 3.6 per cent annually, leaving it well outside the central bank’s preferred range of 2 to 3 per cent and pushing the RBA towards a fifth 0.25-percentage point rate hike this year.
Headline inflation is expected to hit 4.2 per cent annually, rising 0.7 per cent in the quarter.
Mr Ticehurst said rising labour costs would also cause service prices to rise. Commonwealth Bank chief economist Luke Yeaman said that, given high spending across all tiers of federal, state and local government, now 28.9 per cent of the economy, households would have to bear the burden of reducing inflation. “With heavily constrained supply, high public spending and strong AI-led investment, household demand will need to do the heavy lifting to bring demand back below supply,” he said. “The latest hike was always going to be unpopular and politically sensitive.” MORE REPORTS P4 EDITORIAL P10
